open_obligations: Check how closely Brown-Cohen et al.'s formal debate, in which both provers send a message each round and a verifier V with oracle access outputs zero or one, matches Irving et al.'s game with alternating statements and a judge.
Note that inference-time trust in A depends on B being a capable opponent.
Check how many human verifier queries training actually needs.

Note that the judge's role differs: in Irving et al.'s question-answering game a human judge sees the whole debate and decides which agent wins, while in Brown-Cohen et al. actual human raters answer only the verifier's oracle queries during training, and no human feedback is used at inference, when the model is asked to solve a problem or follow complex natural language instructions.
out.other_title: Definition of the two-agent debate game (answers, alternating statements, judge)
out.rationale: Irving et al. define debate as a zero-sum game in which each agent maximises its probability of winning. Brown-Cohen et al. define a debate, citing Irving et al., as a triple (A, B, V) of oracle Turing machines with an oracle O and a common input, in which provers A and B exchange messages over k rounds and the verifier V then outputs zero or one. Their training mapping has pretrained debaters trained by self-play to win the zero-sum game given by the debate protocol, with human labels only for verifier queries, and trusts A's output at inference unless B aborts or points out a flaw; this relies on the debate they credit to Irving et al., in their own formalisation.
out.scope: proposed DEPENDS_ON: training debaters by self-play on the zero-sum game given by a debate, which Brown-Cohen et al. define citing Irving et al., and, at inference, trusting A's output unless B aborts or points out a flaw

text: The authors map the model to practice: debaters A and B are pretrained models trained by self-play on the zero-sum debate game, prover oracle queries are answered from the models' own knowledge of human judgement, and only verifier queries go to actual human raters, so training cost in human judgements equals the number of verifier queries. At inference time the protocol is still run without human feedback, and A's output is trusted as long as B does not abort or point out a flaw.
title: Training and inference with debate: human labels needed only for verifier queries
